verdict.rationale: Daytona documents that each sandbox gets a dedicated kernel, filesystem, network stack and allocated resources, and it offers VM sandboxes with a dedicated Linux or Windows VM, which is a hardware-virtualized boundary. However, the docs also describe container sandboxes, so hard VM-level isolation is not clearly guaranteed for every sandbox, and the boundary is documented only at a high level. Missing for 10: no documented isolation technology or hypervisor (microVM type, gVisor/Kata/Firecracker), no clarity on whether default container sandboxes get the same hard boundary, no published threat model or escape-mitigation details, and no independent or hands-on corroboration of the isolation.

support.subject: As a platform-engineer, I can rely on a documented hard isolation boundary (microVM or equivalent) between sandboxes and my systems

citations.quote: Each sandbox runs in isolation, giving it a dedicated kernel, filesystem, network stack, and allocated vCPU, RAM, and disk.
Daytona also provides VM sandboxes with a dedicated Linux VM or Windows operating system
container sandboxes capture filesystem state only (cold snapshots), VM sandboxes capture filesystem and memory state (hot snapshots)
